questions.question: What is meant by power of accommodation of the eye?
answer_steps: It is the ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length.
This lets the eye focus clearly on both near and distant objects; the ciliary muscles change the curvature of the lens.

questions.question: A person with a myopic eye cannot see objects beyond 1.2 m distinctly. What should be the type of the corrective lens used to restore proper vision?
answer_steps: A concave (diverging) lens.
Its focal length should be 1.2 m (f = −1.2 m, power about −0.83 D), so that distant objects appear to be at the far point.

questions.question: What is the far point and near point of the human eye with normal vision?
answer_steps: Near point: about 25 cm from the eye.
Far point: infinity.

questions.question: A student has difficulty reading the blackboard while sitting in the last row. What could be the defect the child is suffering from? How can it be corrected?
answer_steps: Myopia (near-sightedness): distant objects look blurred.
It is corrected with spectacles having a concave lens of suitable power.

questions.question: The human eye can focus on objects at different distances by adjusting the focal length of the eye lens. This is due to
questions.explanation: Adjusting the focal length to see near and far is accommodation.

questions.question: The human eye forms the image of an object at its
questions.explanation: The image is formed on the retina.

questions.question: The least distance of distinct vision for a young adult with normal vision is about
questions.explanation: The near point of a normal eye is about 25 cm.

questions.question: The change in focal length of an eye lens is caused by the action of the
questions.explanation: The ciliary muscles change the curvature of the lens.
option_feedback: The pupil only lets light in.
The iris controls the pupil size.

questions.question: A person needs a lens of power –5.5 dioptres for correcting his distant vision. For correcting his near vision he needs a lens of power +1.5 dioptre. What is the focal length of the lens required for correcting (i) distant vision, and (ii) near vision?
answer_steps: (i) $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{-5.5}$ m $\approx -0.182$ m $= -18.2$ cm (concave lens)
(ii) $f = \dfrac{1}{1.5}$ m $\approx 0.667$ m $= 66.7$ cm (convex lens)

questions.question: The far point of a myopic person is 80 cm in front of the eye. What is the nature and power of the lens required to correct the problem?
answer_steps: A concave lens with $f = -80$ cm $= -0.8$ m is needed.

questions.question: Make a diagram to show how hypermetropia is corrected. The near point of a hypermetropic eye is 1 m. What is the power of the lens required to correct this defect? Assume that the near point of the normal eye is 25 cm.
answer_steps: A convex lens must form a virtual image of an object at 25 cm at the near point, 1 m: $u = -25$ cm, $v = -100$ cm
$\dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{100} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{3}{100}$, so $f = \dfrac{100}{3}$ cm $\approx 0.33$ m
$P = \dfrac{1}{f} = +3$ D. (Diagram: without the lens the image of a near object forms behind the retina; the convex lens brings it onto the retina.)

questions.question: Why is a normal eye not able to see clearly the objects placed closer than 25 cm?
answer_steps: The focal length of the eye lens cannot be decreased below a certain limit: the ciliary muscles cannot make it any thicker.
So the image of an object closer than 25 cm forms behind the retina and looks blurred.

questions.question: What happens to the image distance in the eye when we increase the distance of an object from the eye?
answer_steps: The image distance does not change: it is the distance from the lens to the retina, which is fixed.
Instead, the eye lens changes its focal length (accommodation) so that the image still forms on the retina.

questions.question: Why do stars twinkle?
answer_steps: Starlight is refracted continuously as it passes through layers of air of changing refractive index (atmospheric refraction).
Since the star is very far away, it acts as a point source, and its apparent position keeps shifting slightly.
The amount of light entering the eye also keeps changing, so the star seems to flicker: it twinkles.

questions.question: Explain why the planets do not twinkle.
answer_steps: Planets are much closer to the earth and look like extended sources: a collection of many point sources of light.
The variations in light from all these points average out to zero, so there is no twinkling.

questions.question: Why does the sky appear dark instead of blue to an astronaut?
answer_steps: At very great heights there is almost no atmosphere, so there are no particles to scatter sunlight.
No scattered light reaches the astronaut's eyes from the sky, so it looks dark.

questions.question: Choose the correct option from the below which explains the reason for us to perceive the day sky as blue.
options: As sunlight passes through the atmosphere, shorter wavelengths, such as blue are scattered more than other colors.
The sky appears blue because all colors are scattered equally, but blue light is stronger and more visible to the human eye.
The blue color of the sky is due to longer wavelengths like red and orange scattering more than shorter wavelengths, making blue stand out more.
The atmosphere contains blue-colored particles that give the sky its blue appearance.
questions.explanation: Fine air molecules scatter short wavelengths (blue) much more than long ones; our eyes are more sensitive to blue than violet.
option_feedback: Longer wavelengths are scattered less, not more.

questions.question:
(i) What is dispersion of light?

(ii) Explain the condition under which dispersion happens.

(iii) Give one reason that causes presbyopia.
answer_steps: (i) Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its component colours (spectrum) when it passes through a medium such as a prism.
(ii) It happens when light enters a medium in which the speed, and so the refractive index, is different for different colours; each colour then bends by a different angle.
(iii) With age, the ciliary muscles weaken and the eye lens loses its flexibility.

questions.question: The crystalline lens of people at old age becomes milky and cloudy. This condition is called ____.
questions.explanation: A milky, cloudy eye lens is cataract, treated by surgery.

questions.question: State whether the following statement is true or false: The twinkling of a star is due to atmospheric refraction of starlight.
questions.explanation: Changing refraction in the moving atmosphere keeps shifting the star's apparent position and brightness.
option_feedback: Correct! Changing refraction in the moving atmosphere keeps shifting the star's apparent position and brightness.
Not quite. Changing refraction in the moving atmosphere keeps shifting the star's apparent position and brightness.

questions.question: In the dispersion of white light through a prism, which coloured light bends the least?
questions.explanation: Red bends the least; violet bends the most.

questions.question:
(a) Define power of accommodation of eye.

(b) Write the function of ciliary muscle.
answer_steps: (a) The ability of the eye lens to adjust its focal length to see near and far objects clearly.
(b) The ciliary muscles change the curvature, and so the focal length, of the eye lens.

questions.question: Explain the differences between myopia and hypermetropia.
answer_steps: Myopia: far objects look blurred; the far point is nearer than infinity. Hypermetropia: near objects look blurred; the near point is farther than 25 cm.
Myopia: the image forms in front of the retina (lens too curved or eyeball too long). Hypermetropia: the image forms behind the retina (focal length too long or eyeball too small).
Myopia is corrected with a concave lens; hypermetropia with a convex lens.

questions.question: The part of the eye that controls the size of the pupil is the:
questions.explanation: The iris adjusts the size of the pupil.
option_feedback: It carries signals to the brain.
The cornea is the clear front surface.

questions.question: The image formed on the retina is:
questions.explanation: The convex eye lens forms a real, inverted image; the brain interprets it.
option_feedback: A virtual image cannot form on a screen.
A convex lens gives an inverted real image.
The image on the retina is real.

questions.question: Hypermetropia is corrected by using a:
questions.explanation: A convex lens brings the image of near objects onto the retina.
option_feedback: Plane glass does not change focus.
Mirrors are not used in spectacles.

questions.question: Bifocal lenses are generally used to correct:
questions.explanation: The upper part corrects distant vision, the lower part near vision.
option_feedback: A simple concave lens corrects myopia alone.

questions.question: The colour of white light that deviates the most through a prism is:
questions.explanation: Violet bends the most; red the least.

questions.question: A rainbow is always seen:
options: in the direction opposite to the Sun
questions.explanation: Sunlight is dispersed and internally reflected by raindrops back towards the observer.
option_feedback: The light comes back from the droplets.
Rainbows are usually seen in the morning or evening.

questions.question: The Sun is visible about 2 minutes before actual sunrise because of:
questions.explanation: Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight over the horizon.

questions.explanation: Being scattered least, red light reaches far.

Then it could not be seen far.

questions.explanation: Smoke particles scatter the light: the Tyndall effect.
option_feedback: That needs a denser medium boundary.

questions.question: Write the functions of the iris and the retina.
answer_steps: Iris: controls the size of the pupil, and so the amount of light entering the eye.
Retina: a light-sensitive screen on which the image forms; its cells send signals through the optic nerve to the brain.

questions.question: Why does the Sun look reddish at sunrise and sunset?
answer_steps: Near the horizon, sunlight passes through a much thicker layer of air.
Most of the blue light is scattered away on the way, so mainly red light reaches our eyes.

questions.question: How is a rainbow formed? Where is it seen?
answer_steps: After rain, tiny water droplets in the air act like small prisms.
Sunlight is refracted and dispersed on entering a droplet, reflected internally, and refracted again on leaving.
The colours reach the observer; a rainbow is seen in the sky opposite the Sun.

questions.question: What is the Tyndall effect? How does the size of particles decide the colour of scattered light?
answer_steps: The scattering of light by colloidal particles, which makes the path of a beam visible, is the Tyndall effect (e.g. sunbeams in a forest).
Very fine particles scatter mainly blue (short wavelength) light.
Larger particles scatter longer wavelengths; very large ones scatter all colours equally, so they look white (clouds).

questions.question: What is myopia? Give its two causes. How is it corrected? Find the power of the corrective lens for a person whose far point is 2 m.
answer_steps: Myopia: a person can see near objects clearly but not distant ones; the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina.
Causes: excessive curvature of the eye lens; elongation of the eyeball.
Correction: a concave lens of suitable power, which makes parallel rays appear to come from the far point.

questions.question: Explain, with reasons: (a) twinkling of stars (b) advance sunrise and delayed sunset (c) blue colour of the sky.
answer_steps: (a) Starlight is refracted by layers of air whose refractive index keeps changing; the star, a point source, appears to shift and its brightness varies, so it twinkles.
The apparent position of a star is also slightly higher than its actual position.
(b) Atmospheric refraction bends sunlight over the horizon, so the Sun is seen about 2 minutes before sunrise and after sunset.
(c) Air molecules are much smaller than the wavelength of visible light and scatter blue light more than red.
This scattered blue light reaches our eyes from all parts of the sky.

questions.question:
At a school eye camp, Mihir could read the eye chart only from very close, while his grandmother could read the far chart but needed to hold her newspaper at arm's length.

(i) Which defect does Mihir have? (1)

(ii) Which lens will correct Mihir's vision? (1)

(iii) What defect does the grandmother probably have, and why does it happen? OR Her near point is 50 cm. Find the power of the lens she needs to read at 25 cm. (2)
answer_steps: (i) Myopia (near-sightedness).
(ii) A concave lens.

(iii) Presbyopia: with age, the ciliary muscles weaken and the eye lens becomes less flexible. OR $u = -25$ cm, $v = -50$ cm: $\dfrac{1}{f} = -\dfrac{1}{50} + \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{1}{50}$, $f = 0.5$ m, $P = +2$ D (convex lens).

questions.question:
On a trip to the hills, Ananya passed sunlight through a glass prism and saw a band of colours on the wall. In the evening the Sun looked orange-red, and at night the stars twinkled while Jupiter shone steadily.

(i) What is the band of colours called? (1)

(ii) Which colour bent the most? (1)

(iii) Why did the Sun look orange-red in the evening? OR Why did Jupiter not twinkle? (2)
answer_steps: (i) The spectrum (formed by dispersion).
(ii) Violet.

(iii) Near the horizon, sunlight travels through a thick layer of air, and most of the blue is scattered away, leaving mainly red and orange. OR Jupiter is an extended source; the variations in light from its many points average out.
